paragraphs.text: This is [Oriental Beauty](hsinchu:why-people-value-it) from [Hsinchu](hsinchu:where-it-is), a county of hills and uplands in the north west of Taiwan. Tea there is largely a [Hakka](hsinchu:hakka) trade: local families grow the leaf, make the tea and sell it, and many farms have passed down through generations. The record names the county but not a township, and the county covers several tea townships, among them [Emei and Beipu](hsinchu:tea-townships).

The tea depends on a [small green leafhopper](hsinchu:summer-leafhopper) that feeds on the young shoots in summer. Its bite starts the leaf's change while it is still on the bush, so growers keep insecticide off these gardens. The bud and the next two leaves are picked by hand, and the leaf is [oxidised far more](taiwan-oolong:oriental-beauty) than other Taiwan oolong, close to red tea, before it is dried. Locally it keeps an older folk name, [pengfeng cha](hsinchu:oriental-beauty-names), braggart's tea.

brewing.text: Ball-rolled Taiwan oolong takes hot water, about 90 to 100°C, a fairly generous amount of leaf and short steeps; the balls open slowly and give many infusions. Roasted Dong Ding takes water from about 95°C to a full boil. Aged oolong takes very hot water, in a pot that holds its heat, clay above all. Oriental Beauty is the exception and takes cooler water, about 80 to 95°C.

notice.text: In light high mountain tea: a sweet, floral cup, often creamy or buttery, with little bitterness and a long sweet aftertaste. In roasted Dong Ding: caramel, ripe fruit, nuts and a toasted aroma. In Baozhong: floral notes and a clear, bright liquor. In Oriental Beauty: ripe fruit and honey, with little bitterness.
